articles.title: Canadian Politician Wants the Government to Help BioWare Staff Buy the Studio From EA and Run It Themselves
articles.summary: Avi Lewis, leader of one of Canada's top opposition parties, wants the Canadian government to save Mass Effect developer BioWare.
articles.body:
Avi Lewis, leader of one of Canada's top opposition parties, wants the Canadian government to help save Mass Effect developer BioWare. The leader of the New Democratic Party took to social media to speak out against publisher EA.

On October 21, EA announced a major shift in strategy and a significant internal restructuring that involves the cancellation of a number of projects, the closure of BioWare in Edmonton , and a reported 400 people losing their jobs. The studio, known for franchises like Mass Effect and Dragon Age, was shut down after more than 30 years of creating beloved role-playing games. It reportedly had 50 people working on the next Mass Effect, all of which were cut.

Lewis linked BioWare's closure to the $55 billion EA acquisition by an investor group composed of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, Silver Lake, and Affinity Partners, approved in December 2025. Since the acquisition, EA has been focusing only on its biggest brands — Battlefield and its sports titles, predominantly — while other series have been pushed aside.

11 Mass Effect Characters and Moments the TV Show Needs to Be a Hit

"This is private equity, this is what it does. Buy up businesses, run them into the ground, and rip them apart for short-term profit," Lewis wrote on X / Twitter .

"The developers at BioWare know how to run the studio. They know how to make the games we all love. They should be given the first opportunity — and the federal support — to buy it and run it themselves. And if we want to avoid the Mass Effect effect in Canada, we should be keeping private equity out, not welcoming it in."

It’s not a huge surprise that a Canadian official would be plugged into the games industry. Canada already offers significant federal and provincial tax relief to support video game development studios, offsetting costs, which is why so many studios set up a permanent base in major Canadian cities. It’s a government that’s traditionally understood the value gaming brings to a modern economy.

One question fans have is whether or not EA might be willing to sell off BioWare franchises such as Mass Effect and Dragon Age to another studio. IGN spoke to a number of video game industry analysts to find out whether that was likely, and why EA decided to close BioWare down .

A day after EA's announcement, a trailer for the canceled Mass Effect leaked online . It showed alien smooching, blue tentacle-headed women, and included a title for the game: Mass Effect Universe.

BioWare was a hugely influential studio and basically invented RPG conversation wheels, which have become standard in the genre. Upcoming games The Expanse: Osiris Reborn and Exodus both owe a lot to Mass Effect .

Kirk McKeand is a Contributor on IGN News. Find him on Twitter @MckKirk

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto V – The Legacy Review
articles.summary: GTA V was a game so preposterously future-proof upon its 2013 launch that its subsequent ports to modern machines have remained the benchmark for open-world action-driving games.
articles.body:
I’m taking a look back at each of the core Grand Theft Auto games and replaying them in the lead-up to the arrival of Grand Theft Auto 6. What we’ll be putting together won’t be traditional re-reviews, and they won’t come with any new IGN score, but they will re-examine what made each GTA remarkable upon the time of its release. By the end of the project, using GTA’s previously six-star wanted level, you should be able to get an idea of where each of these games roughly rank in my long-term love for this series.

Our last stop in this series is Grand Theft Auto V: a game so nice, they released it thrice.

13 years. Three console generations. 230 million copies. Over $10 billion in revenue. The numbers that tell the story of Grand Theft Auto V’s longevity and success are wildly impressive and virtually unprecedented. The only other games even in the conversation are Minecraft or, depending on your criteria, about 200 different versions of Tetris. The numbers, however, don’t tell us why GTA V still sells more copies every few months than most games will ever total. They don’t tell us why people can’t get enough of it, and they don’t tell us why it’s special. So how did we get here? I guess it was the weather.

While GTA IV’s Liberty City sandbox was a dense, modestly-sized, and entirely urban environment, GTA V’s vision of the city of Los Santos was considerably more sprawling and varied. Yes, it retained a grid-like downtown district packed with tall buildings and a few particularly sizable skyscrapers, but Los Santos otherwise has a wholly different identity to that of Liberty City – and the map encompasses an area way beyond Los Santos itself.

The aesthetic shift is stark. Weather depending, the beating San Andreas sunshine gives vehicles a dazzling gleam, casts crisp shadows, and saturates the whole place with a sharp, sun-bleached vibe. It’s not the stylised orange tint that illustrated the oppressive heat of 1992 Los Santos in GTA: San Andreas, but it’s bright, effective, and a striking visual departure from the cold, drab, and gritty appearance of Liberty City.

It’s also such a different place to explore. The town is splintered into dozens of distinct districts that seamlessly blend from one to the next – from the affluent mansions of Vinewood Hills and Richman to the spectacle of Vinewood itself, glowing under a thin layer of grime and entertainment industry sleaze, and from the sun-kissed sand and beach bum backalleys of ageing Vespucci to the graffiti-tagged and struggling suburbs of South Los Santos.

Outside Los Santos, the countryside opens up to include desert, forest, mountains, and a handful of other small towns dotted around the map. It’s essentially a greatly expanded vision of the southern segment of GTA: San Andreas’ map – the section that features Los Santos, Mount Chiliad, and its immediate surroundings. It’s actually more than twice the size of GTA: San Andreas in its entirety, even if it doesn’t always feel that way, considering you can’t travel beyond the fringe of the county to find a fully-fledged San Fierro or Las Venturas. However, that’s more of a statement about how utterly special GTA: San Andreas’ map really is, rather than an indictment of GTA V in any real way.

That is, GTA V’s map remains a stunning achievement. It’s a world that – even after 13 years – I’m still spotting signs, storefronts, and subtleties that I don’t think I’ve overtly noticed before. Like all the best developers, Rockstar understands that true immersion emerges through accumulation: a single graffiti-tagged wall, bill-covered pole, or interesting piece of architecture might not be hugely remarkable on its own, but combined they become something else altogether. Funnily enough, a world full of thousands of such details can make an entire city so realistic you essentially stop noticing it. It’s almost counterintuitive; things don’t stand out, because they look so authentic, lived-in, and normal .

The smartest way Rockstar exploits this densely detailed map is through GTA V’s defining innovation: its trio of protagonists. You swap between Michael De Santa, a retired criminal becoming increasingly agitated at his otherwise comfortable suburban life; Franklin Clinton, an aspiring, small-time hustler looking for a real payday to get him out of his rundown neighbourhood; and Trevor Philips, a wildly volatile Canadian psychopath who was formerly partners with Michael.

The system is much more than a novelty. Switching between them allows Rockstar to prod us into different parts of the world to explore, without relying on a single character to experience everything. For a map this large, it makes a lot of sense.

For clarity, following the release of its single-player expansions The Lost and Damned and The Ballad of Gay Tony, GTA IV also ultimately featured three protagonists – and three different lenses through which we could view and interact with Liberty City. Similarly, it was a really smart way of squeezing more value out of the map, and drilling down on parts of it Niko Bellic’s story never really took him to. But while you could certainly regard this as a first draft of a multi-protagonist approach, you can’t switch between them in real time in GTA IV; you have to pause and load into the expansions separately.

In GTA V, the transition between characters is far, far more rapid, and occurs after just a brief zoom out and back in again, dropping you into Michael, Franklin, or Trevor’s life in the middle of whatever they happen to be doing at the time – which may well be dropping a man off a bridge. The transitions give the illusion that these guys continue to exist beyond the missions in which they appear.

GTA V’s missions are typically far more varied and layered than those in GTA IV. After experimenting with it in The Ballad of Gay Tony, GTA V introduced mission checkpoints and finally shed what had arguably become the most frustrating characteristic of the series – the need to completely start from scratch after failing a mission.

This is what allows GTA V’s missions to be longer and regularly more wild than ever. With checkpoints as a safety net, Rockstar could really push the boat out with what it asked us to attempt – free from the sometimes debilitating concern that messing up at the last minute will result in a long drive and a lot of backtracking over things we’ve already done.

Of course, the highlight here is the focus on multilayed heists, taking the fan-favourite Three Leaf Clover bank robbery mission from GTA IV and blowing that concept out to make it the central pillar of GTA V’s campaign. There are multiple big scores that can be tackled in overtly different ways, something made easy to experiment with thanks to the ability to easily replay missions from a list of those you’ve previously completed. With the exception of The Ballad of Gay Tony, in past GTA games, the only way to play the missions again was to start over from the beginning.

The heists are where the three-character structure becomes most effective. We’re not just passengers on these huge marquee missions; rather, GTA V builds elaborate on ramps to these heists focused on planning and preparation which typically draw on the different skills and traits of Michael, Franklin, and Trevor. It gives the heists, and the campaign as a whole, a sense of scale and variety that would’ve been difficult to achieve through a single character.

Beyond the multiple protagonists and the escalation in mission variety, GTA V also made major changes to the car handling and significant refinements to the shooting. Vehicles are certainly more approachable to drive in GTA V than they are in GTA IV; they brake hard and respond sharply to steering input. The result isn’t superficial or overly light, but it does feel very grippy. It’s a handling model that I think is particularly suited to sure-footed sports cars, although I have to concede a part of me prefers the way older vehicles feel with the “slidey cars” cheat on. It’s just more drift-friendly.

In terms of vehicle variety, however, GTA V is very much a welcome shift back to the broad spectrum available in GTA: San Andreas after things were scaled back significantly in GTA IV. As a result, one minute you could be fanging an 18-wheeler down the freeway, and the next kicking tyres and lighting fires in a fighter jet. GTA V dialled things up rather than back, so go ahead: land that jumbo on the beach and escape via a jet ski. Why the hell not?

Combat was polished too, with more nimble movement and more dependable cover shooting. The highlight for me is the sound of firefights, as guns bark and bullets thunk into car panels. It’s brilliant stuff. The integration of the weapon wheel, which functions similarly to Red Dead Redemption and Max Payne 3, also means you can carry way more hardware – as well as multiple weapons within a single class. The weapon wheel stores all of the weapons you collect and you’ll never lose them, even if they run out of ammo or you get busted.

When GTA V launched on Xbox 360 and PS3 in September 2013, both of those consoles were approaching the end of their lifespans. With the Xbox One and PS4 arriving in November that same year, you could probably make a strong case that GTA V felt like the last great statement of that generation. Many people did. However, I think there’s more to it than that.

A couple of weeks before its September 17 release, I was fortunate enough to conduct the world’s first hands-on with GTA V for IGN . Revisiting and playing it again so extensively this week has very effectively taken me back to how blown away I was in that moment. I was stunned by what I was playing, and utterly convinced GTA V was outright good enough to upstage both Microsoft and Sony’s new consoles. In fact, I wrote never mind November; the next generation will start when Rockstar says it does. In 2013, that was a comment reflective of just how ahead of its time I believed GTA V was; that it was simply streets ahead of its peers, squeezing next-generation scope and ambition out of a console that first launched in 2005. Simply put, it felt like a new benchmark for an era that hadn’t even officially arrived yet. On September 3, 2013 – two weeks before GTA V came out – maybe that’s a bold claim. But with new and improved versions of GTA V going on to loom large over the generation to follow, and then doing it all over again for the generation after that – all to the tune of 230 million copies – I don’t think it was ever an exaggeration.

Grand Theft Auto V was a game so preposterously future-proof upon its 2013 launch on Xbox 360 and PS3 that its subsequent ports to modern machines remain the benchmark for open-world action-driving games. At the conclusion of this GTA Legacy Review project I find myself too emotionally attached to the PS2 pair of Vice City and San Andreas to push past my adoration for the style and soundtracks of those period piece classics and place anything above them but, make no mistake, there are very few games I’ve played more than GTA V. Combining an enormous and extraordinarily detailed world, three compelling protagonists, a thrilling set of varied missions and heists, and the foundation for a world of multiplayer that is simply a whole separate discussion, GTA V is the peak of the series. At least for the next few weeks, that is.

For more reflections on the incredible Grand Theft Auto series, you can read our new Legacy Reviews of Grand Theft Auto , Grand Theft Auto 2 , Grand Theft Auto III , Grand Theft Auto: Vice City , Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas , and Grand Theft Auto IV .

Luke Reilly is an award-winning journalist with 23 years of media experience. He previously served as Editor of Official PlayStation Magazine – Australia and Australian 360, before joining IGN in 2011. You can find him on Bluesky @mrlukereilly to ask him things about stuff.

articles.title: Arkane Lyon Reportedly Could Be Closed in Mid-November if a Buyer Isn't Found, With Marvel's Blade Still in Development
articles.summary: Arkane Lyon is still working on Marvel’s Blade, but it’s doing it with the Sword of Damocles dangling over the heads of its 217 employees.
articles.body:
Arkane Lyon is still working on Marvel’s Blade, but it’s doing it with the Sword of Damocles dangling over the heads of its 217 employees.

According to French outlet Le Monde , Florange Law, adopted in 2014 in France, requires companies with more than 1,000 employees to search for a buyer for at least three months before closing a studio. According to the report, the search for a buyer for the Dishonored 2 and Deathloop developer began in the summer, meaning the deadline is imminent — November 13.

The studio was informed of Microsoft’s decision on July 16, shortly after new Xbox CEO Asha Sharma announced closure or spinoff plans for Compulsion Games, Double Fine Productions, Ninja Theory, and Undead Labs — Ninja Theory was closed while the other studios went independent, taking their franchises with them. Over 1,600 jobs were affected across Microsoft's gaming business at the time. More have followed, and more are set to follow still.

Every Video Game Franchise Xbox Owns After Acquiring Activision Blizzard

According to Le Monde, a union rep said that "negotiations on the redundancy plan are going badly” at Arkane Lyon, which Microsoft picked up when it bought Bethesda owner ZeniMax in 2021. The worker unions are currently trying to buy more time "to give the discussions a better chance of reaching a conclusion."

“Several forms of takeover are being considered,” according to the report, which suggests buyers are interested in the immersive sim studio. That’s why the union is pushing for more time and is “hopeful of saving the studio and its jobs.”

Microsoft didn’t respond directly to the report but sent the following statement: "We continue to explore different options for Arkane as part of the ongoing French consultation process. We are keeping the works council and employees informed and are actively seeking a partner to support the next phase of development and enable the commercialization of the project."

An internal document seen by Le Monde stated that "the implementation of the project [for the complete and definitive cessation of the company's activities] is scheduled to begin at the end of 2026 and should extend into the first quarter of 2027."

The union is currently pushing for re-employment of affected staff to other studios within Xbox. "The redundancy plan must be adapted to the video game market where, currently, the prospects for returning to work are extremely limited,” said the rep.

Negotiations are ongoing until October 30, but the union hasn’t ruled out seeing Microsoft in court. “This is in complete contradiction with what we've been told in the Works Council for years about the company's financial situation," the rep said. "Microsoft is looking to divest itself of Arkane, even though the studio is doing well, in order to save money and improve the profitability of its short-term investments."

Through all of this is concern that Marvel's Blade may never see the light of day. IGN understands that prior to the layoffs in July, Blade was on track for a reveal early next year and a release in the fourth quarter of 2027. IGN has asked Marvel Games for comment but it has failed to respond.

Blade was announced in December 2023 with a reveal trailer, but we've seen nothing of it since. In June, Bethesda Game Studios head Todd Howard was quoted as saying he'd recently seen what Arkane Lyon was cooking up and was impressed . "I'm not at liberty to say when [we'll see more]," Howard teased at the time, "but I saw some stuff just yesterday [on May 21] and the folks at Arkane [Studios, the developers] are doing a really, really great job."

Kirk McKeand is a Contributor on IGN News. Find him on Twitter @MckKirk

articles.title: The Simpsons Halloween Episodes: Every 'Treehouse of Horror' Special, Ranked
articles.summary: Using the power of The Shinning and twirling towards freedom, we rank every "Treehouse of Horror" special from Season 2 to Season 38.
articles.body:
Can any TV series rival The Simpsons for the sheer number of Halloween episodes ? Since Season 2, the series has given fans at least one new "Treehouse of Horror" anthology episode every single year. Early on, these stories were more directly horror-centric, but since then "Treehouse of Horror" has become something of a clearinghouse for stuff the writers can't do during a "regular" episode. And we love it. Well, usually...

In honor of this Halloween tradition, we've ranked every single "Treehouse of Horror" episode so far, up through Season 38's "Treehouse of Horror Presents: The Revengening." Some of them are good enough to rival the best episodes from the show's golden years. Others… well, it's hard to bat a thousand over three decades. Read on for our full list, and after you're done, be sure to check out our recently updated best Simpsons Episodes list and see a preview of a classic Treehouse of Horror comic .

And be sure to check back soon to see where the upcoming "Treehouse of Horror XXXVII" ranks on the list.

The Simpsons: Every Treehouse of Horror Episode Ranked

"The Diving Bell and the Butterball" is the single-worst "Treehouse of Horror" segment ever, and it's not particularly close. It's essentially one long, profoundly unfunny fart joke. The final segment is an Avatar parody that, like Avatar, has not aged well.

We'll give this episode a slight bit of credit for trying to shake up the formula and tackle five segments instead of the usual three. But predictably, that only means this batch of horror spoofs feels even more rushed and underdeveloped than usual. The biggest disappointment here is "Bong Joon Ho's 'This Side of Parasite,'" which adds absolutely nothing to the satirical horror film it lampoons.

Guillermo del Toro was responsible for the opening sequence of this episode, but after that it's really bland. None of the segments are good in the slightest. In particular, the second segment, "Dead and Shoulders," involves Bart's head being attached to Lisa's body, which is a trope that has been handled seemingly dozens of times before, including in a previous "Treehouse of Horror" episode.

This episode is particularly frustrating in that it probably could have been a winner had the concepts been fleshed out more. "Toy Gory" is a deeply uninspired spoof of the Toy Story movies, and "Be Nine, Rewind" misses the mark with its time travel humor. This episode does at least have the somewhat amusing Marvel parody "Into the Homer-Verse," but even that ultimately recycles a similar premise from the much more successful "Treehouse of Horror XIII."

This is another case where the gorgeously animated opening sequence (in this case courtesy of The Book of Life's Jorge R. Gutierrez) is more memorable than any of the actual segments. "The Information Rage" is a mostly toothless satire of society's current political divide disguised as a Pacific Rim parody, while "Denim" is a so-so sendup of the Venom movies. "The Fall of the House of Monty" packs a bit more punch, feeling like a return to a more classic type of "Treehouse of Horror" tale.

"The Others" is a fun segment where the "ghosts" of the original Simpsons designs haunt the current Simpson family. It's fun to hear Dan Castellaneta do his old Walter Matthau-esque Homer voice again. On the other hand, "School is Hell" is an example of an unfortunate trend that started to plague these episodes as things went on; super gory gross-out humor that is unsubtle and unpleasant. Call it a mixed bag.

This recent addition to the series is so unmemorable you may very well not recall a single segment. That means none of them are particularly good, but also none of them are particularly bad. It's thoroughly mediocre. Also, this is the 600th episode, which feels unfortunate, but it did get us a semi-fun song tacked onto the end. You'd like such a significant milestone to be marked by something other than a bland collection of stories that includes an uninspired James Bond/Kingsman parody.

This episode is another real mixed bag. The segment spoofing NFTs and Crypto Bros feels dated on arrival, and the Kylie Jenner cameo doesn't help. "Lout Break" is a half-hearted spoof of pandemic movies that never really connects. But there is fun to be had in "Ei8ht," as the series again brings in Kelsey Grammer's Sideshow Bob for a story set in an alternate universe where the beloved episode "Cape Feare" ended very differently.

This is another "just OK" episode that's bolstered by a strong opening sequence (in this case courtesy of The Onion's Stan Kelly). Of the three segments, the one real standout is "Plastic World." The novel 3D animation style and the unlikely fusion of Waterworld and Mad Max make for a pretty amusing tale of a Springfield overrun by plastic waste.

The 30th Treehouse special also happens to be the show's 666th episode, a fact that yields some comedic gold in the Omen-inspired intro sequence. Beyond that, however, there's not much to write home about with this one, even as The Simpsons finally gets around to spoofing Netflix's Stranger Things in "Danger Things."

Sideshow Bob finally got to kill Bart. That's amusing in concept, although the segment isn't actually all that enjoyable. For such a "momentous" event, it didn't really stick the landing. "Homerzilla" is no "King Homer," but it's decent enough. One imagines it can be hard to keep coming up with new "Treehouse of Horror" segments, but it'd be nice for the execution to be a bit higher than these more recent ones, nevertheless.

Like many of the more recent specials, Treehouse XXIX tries and mostly fails to do justice to the classic horror fare it spoofs. It's particularly frustrating seeing the series struggle with classics like Invasion of the Body Snatchers and Jurassic Park (though the latter got all the parody it ever needed way back in Season 6's "Itchy & Scratchy Land"). But this episode does hit paydirt with a much more recent film, as "Multiplisa-ty" turns out to be a surprisingly entertaining riff on M. Night Shyamalan's Split.

"Mr. & Mrs. Simpson" is a parody of Mr. and Mrs. Smith, which has nothing to do with Halloween. However, it's also the best segment in this episode, and a good, entertaining one overall. It's certainly an argument in favor of "Treehouse of Horror" stepping out of the Halloween and horror world. That's also true of the final segment "Heck House," which is definitely spooky, but equally mundane. The opening segment is an E.T. parody that's fine.

26. "Treehouse of Horror Presents: Simpsons Wicked This Way Comes" (2024)

Simpsons fans got a bonus Halloween episode in Season 36, one which turned out to be quite a bit more memorable than the actual "Treehouse of Horror XXXV." This one has the benefit of being united around a common theme, with each installment spoofing a different Ray Bradbury story. The highlight here is definitely the Fahrenheit 451 parody that closes out the episode.

The opening segment is really fun, especially if you like the idea of Frankenstein's Monster dressing like SpongeBob. "Don't Have a Cow, Mankind" is a solid zombie story, although not as good as "Dial 'Z' for Zombies," which we'll talk about in a bit. The final segment is weird, because it's quite meta. It's basically the characters from the show putting on a parody of Sweeney Todd. However, that also makes it feel fresh, which is impressive 20 episodes in.

The clone story is funny, especially the dig at Family Guy they sneaked into it. On the other hand, "The Island of Dr. Hibbert" isn't funny in the slightest, and is one of the worst "Treehouse of Horror" stories. The first two segments are carrying that one to make this a middle-of-the-road outing.

This episode features an of-the-moment parody of Twilight, a very much not-of-the-moment parody of Dead Calm, and a -- now, anyway -- suddenly of-the-moment parody of Jumanji. They are all fine, although the Jumanji bit is surprisingly dark. That is if you consider the idea of two 10-year-olds being hanged dark.

There is a lot of potential in a Harry Potter parody, even in 2001 when that franchise was still mostly known in book form. But "Wiz Kids" only partially succeeds. Pierce Brosnan is fun as the voice of a killer house in "House of Whacks," and the first segment is decent enough. This particular edition of "Treehouse of Horror" came at a time when popular opinion was starting to turn against The Simpsons, and also at a time when these Halloween episodes were airing in early November. Both of these things went against this episode, but time has revealed it as being an OK half-hour of TV.

For a recent Treehouse of Horror installment, this one is unusually decent. "The Pookadook" is a surprisingly effective sendup of The Babadook, and if nothing else, "Death Tome" offers a welcome chance to see the world of Springfield rendered in full-blown anime style. The real highlight here, though, is "Simpsons World," an extremely meta parody of HBO's Westworld series that gleefully and repeatedly calls back to the show's golden era.

"The Day the Earth Looked Stupid," a parody of the (alleged) panic stemming from Orson Welles' "War of the Worlds" broadcast, has an interesting idea it doesn't execute in ideal fashion. It does eventually turn into a satire of America's invasion of Iraq, which you would think would date things, but… On the other hand, Richard Lewis voicing a neurotic golem is quite funny. Then Fran Drescher shows up and this Halloween episode gets rather Jewish (to its tremendous benefit).

"The Ned Zone" is really good, because it builds on Ned Flanders' mild-mannered personality, and also his sometimes antagonistic relationship with Homer. When a story is a flight of fancy, it's a lot easier to accept Homer being a complete jerk and doofus, and the stakes can be higher. Like, the destruction of Springfield through nuclear meltdown higher. The other two segments are pretty good, and we do get to hear Yeardley Smith put an English accent onto her Lisa voice.

Here is a case where every single segment could be met with "Eh, I guess that was OK." That makes for a decent episode of television, but also one that is somewhat difficult to discuss critically at length. At least The Simpsons got to take a shot at baseball in its opening sequence. At this time, the MLB playoffs were pushing "Treehouse of Horror" into November, which one imagines the folks on the show weren't too happy about.

This episode is easily among the best of the more recent Treehouse specials. That's thanks in no small part to the fact that the series finally gets around to lampooning The Exorcist (with Maggie as the demonically possessed child, naturally). This episode also gets props for its visually ambitious tribute to Neil Gaiman's Coraline in "Coralisa."

"Reaper Madness" is one of the top 10 "Treehouse of Horror" segments of all time. Maybe even top five. Homer becomes the Grim Reaper, and the story ends with Homer trying to outrun God on a motorcycle in a parody of action chases everywhere. It's hilarious and a delight. On the other hand, the other two segments (including one with the late Jerry Lewis) aren't up to that level. In fact, the final segment kind of blows. This ranking is almost entirely thanks to the excellent "Reaper Madness."

Where it all started. At the time, this idea was fresh. The Simpsons stepping out of their real world and telling stories was remarkable. We were introduced to Kang and Kodos! This is definitely a noteworthy episode. It just isn't quite as funny as other installments. Hey, it was a new idea. They had some kinks to work out. It may have been cool to hear James Earl Jones recite "The Raven" on The Simpsons, but is anybody going to try and argue that segment is funny at all?

A parody of I Know What You Did Last Summer. A story built around Xena: The Warrior Princess. A segment all about Y2K. Yes, this "Treehouse of Horror" is very much of its time. That being said, all these bits are at least pretty good. It has some memorable lines, and features a funny appearance from Tom Arnold. This episode will remind you of the importance of putting your fog lights in, and also maybe make you crave some Sugar Crisp.

13. "Treehouse of Horror Presents: The Revengening" (2026)

Between this episode and "Halloween of Horror," there's a real case to be made that the show's Halloween specials should permanently pivot to one full-length storyline. "The Revengening" delivers a satisfying slasher movie parody that works pretty well as a straightforward (and surprisingly gory) slasher in itself. But this episode has the added benefit of finally bringing back a fan-favorite character and tying things up in an appropriately meta way.

Since the idea of "Treehouse of Horror" was still fresh, The Simpsons decided to put these fantastical stories into context. As such, here Homer, Bart, and Lisa all eat too much candy and then have sugar-induced nightmares. The stories are all strongly geared towards the horror and Halloween theme, which is nice, and the twist at the end of Bart's story (he awakes in horror because he has a tender moment with Homer) is clever.

"Hell Toupee" and "The Terror of Tiny Toon" are both good segments. The latter is particularly strong, because Bart and Lisa are sucked into the television, which leads to a lot of fun stuff, including interactions with a live-action Regis and Kathy Lee. The last segment, though, wherein we find out Maggie is an alien and the family goes on Jerry Springer, is a little lackluster. The overall episode is good, though.

For a later "Treehouse of Horror," this edition is particularly amusing. There is a funny segment where Homer kills celebrities so that their images can be used in ads without their consent. Alas, two of the people he killed are the now actually dead Prince and Neil Armstrong (watch your back, George Clooney). However, the final segment, a violent parody of "It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown," is the highlight. It's a pitch-perfect spoof, but also funny and clever beyond that.

None of these three stories are iconic standouts, but they are all good. The opening sequence, a Munsters parody, is also cool, at least if you remember The Munsters. Homer as a ghost is entertaining, and so is the tale of dolphins rising from the oceans to overtake humanity. Additionally, a Hansel and Gretel parody includes a great twist on the old gag of somebody making up a fake name based on something they see in the room. This feels like one of the first instances of that twist, perhaps the very first.

Maybe this episode is more of an honorable mention, since it's not technically part of the Treehouse series. But considering that it's also one of the best Halloween-themed Simpsons episode of the 21st Century, it really deserves a place here. "Halloween of Horror" bucks the anthology format for a single, more straightforward story about Homer trying to help a badly spooked Lisa learn how to enjoy the holiday again. It's a surprisingly heartfelt celebration of their father/daughter bond.

For all the talk of "Treehouse of Horror" getting away from horror stuff in recent years, that trend really started almost as soon these specials became a thing. The third edition of the series features a (decent enough) parody of King Kong. The other two segments are horror-centric, and also better, including "Dial 'Z' for Zombies," which allows Homer to finally shoot Flanders. The evil Krusty doll story is particularly good, and features Homer's iconic "That's good/That's bad" conversation with a mysterious shopkeeper.

This special proves there's still gold to be found even with the more recent seasons. The middle segment, a Paranormal Activity spoof, is decent, and probably necessary. They couldn't avoid doing a found footage horror parody around this time. Meanwhile, the other two segments are really good, especially for being from the 23rd edition. The first one isn't really a parody. It's just a smart, amusing story about a black hole. Then there is "Bart and Homer's Excellent Adventure," which is one of the best segments ever. There's time travel, Artie Ziff, and "The United Federation of Homers Through History."

The top five really take things to another level. "Fly vs. Fly" is great. It features the hilarious line, "The pants are a dead giveaway." Sure, without context that may not be funny, but in context it's great. Watch the episode. It's wall-to-wall wonderful. Homer as the (seemingly) last man on Earth is also a joy. Even "Easy Bake Coven," which isn't quite as good as the other two segments, is memorable and as satisfying as a caramel cod.

"The Devil and Homer Simpson" is definitely memorable. After all, Homer sells his soul for a donut. It may not be side-splittingly funny (or groin-grabbingly transcendent), but the execution is still a lot of fun. That being said, "Terror at 5 ½ Feet" and "Bart Simpson's Dracula" are both really strong. Plus, there are the wraparounds, which were written by Conan O'Brien. Need you be reminded of the most horrifying painting of all? The one of the dogs playing poker? Of course you don't, because it's iconic (and hilarious).

All of these episodes are great, and feature iconic "Treehouse of Horror" segments. This is the episode where Groundskeeper Willie gets an axe in the back in all three stories. There's the one where the adults of Springfield Elementary kill and eat all the children. Homer building a time machine out of a toaster and experiencing the perils of the butterfly effect is super funny. Then, of course, we can't forget "The Shinning." No TV and no beer make Homer something something…

All three of these segments are impeccable. You can try and quibble with them, but your quibbles are faulty. Lard Lad coming to life to get his donut back? Awesome. Groundskeeper Willie as Freddy Krueger in the segment that gave us the quote "Lousy Smarch Weather?" Fantastic. Homer in 3D? Super cool and incredibly fun, even before he enters the real world (and then enters an erotic cake store). This isn't just a great "Treehouse of Horror." It's one of the very best Simpsons episodes period. And yet, it isn't quite the best "Treehouse of Horror" of the bunch.

That's because of this episode. "The Thing and I," with Bart's long-lost twin Hugo, is really good. So is "The Genesis Tub." However, if we are all being honest, this is mostly about "Citizen Kang." "Citizen Kang" is the best "Treehouse of Horror" segment, hands down. It's brilliant. It's one of the most iconic bits of Simpsons history, period. From beginning to end, it's hilarious and full of memorable moments and lines. "Don't blame me, I voted for Kodos" is one of the quintessential Simpsons lines. Thanks to the power of "Citizen Kang" this is the best of all the "Treehouse of Horror" episodes. Abortions for some, miniature American flags for others!

What's your favorite "Treehouse of Horror" episode? Let's discuss in the comments...

Note: This story was updated on November 4, 2024. It originally ran on April 15, 2018.

Chris Morgan is the author of The Ash Heap of History and The Comic Galaxy of Mystery Science Theater 3000. Wisely or not, he's also on Twitter .

articles.title: EA Appears to Have Quietly Pulled Mass Effect Content From Battlefield 6 Following BioWare Shutdown
articles.summary: EA seems to have quietly pulled a collection of Mass Effect content for Battlefield 6 just days after it shuttered series developer BioWare.
articles.body:
EA seems to have quietly pulled a collection of Mass Effect content for Battlefield 6 just days after it shuttered series developer BioWare.

Battlefield 6 players made a mental note of an incoming Mass Effect collab when themed content was added to cosmetic menus with the launch of Season 5 earlier this month. As captured and shared by fans across social media, the previously locked crossover collection featured some sci-fi weaponry, a Normandy ship weapon charm, and more N7-branded items.

With a Dead Space crossover having been added at the same time and N7 Day just around the corner, fans suspected they wouldn't have to wait long to get their hands on the new content. Some even suggested the surprise drop meant EA might have plans to deliver an update on its long-in-development Mass Effect 5 project . Of course, the controversial game publisher announced just days ago that it had no plans for BioWare or Mass Effect at all .

There's new Mass Effect accessories for Battlefield, probably for N7 Day 👀 — Kala Elizabeth #SaveMassEffect (@kalaelizabeth) October 13, 2026

There's new Mass Effect accessories for Battlefield, probably for N7 Day 👀

The remaining team of developers at the studio were abruptly laid off when the studio was shut down two days ago, October 21, 2026. It was a move that rocked the industry and left both fans and outsiders bewildered as EA also confirmed Mass Effect 5 was canceled, with the series' gaming presence consequently thrown into an indefinite hiatus. Perhaps more confusing was the existence of that Mass Effect content in Battlefield 6, but it didn't take long for DICE and the rest of BioWare's former sister studios at Battlefield Studios to pull the collaboration completely.

Fans quickly discovered EA had quietly removed any mention of the Mass Effect cosmetics in the wake of BioWare's shutdown. Although it's a move that has only further divided a community of gamers already disheartened by EA leadership, it's easy to see why the company swiftly moved to pull the plug.

Continuing to push Mass Effect content on fans mourning the demise of the once-beloved sci-fi RPG franchise would certainly only sour the already-bitter taste in players' mouths. With there likely being no plans for any of the franchise's usual N7 Day festivities come November 7, a relatively small drop of cosmetics would have only added insult to injury.

It would have been an especially painful blow for fans of EA's past considering the publisher already caught flak for its even more prominent Dead Space crossover. Featuring both weapons and even a new mode, Battlefield 6's collab arrived at a time when Dead Space's future as a living, breathing game franchise also remained a mystery. Although franchise followers seem to have enjoyed the mode, many have also lobbed criticism at EA for doing the minimum with some of its most critically acclaimed IP.

Still, there are those who think the Mass Effect cosmetics, which seem to have been finished and ready for launch at any moment, would have still been nice to have. After all, the franchise isn't completely without a plan, at least for now. Amazon's Prime Video, for example, confirmed to IGN its previously announced Mass Effect TV series was still very much in the works following BioWare's closure. There are also those hoping the IP and even some members of its studio's team of developers could find a new home .

11 Mass Effect Characters and Moments the TV Show Needs to Be a Hit

EA was officially acquired by Saudi Arabia's PIF, Silver Lake, and Jared Kushner's Affinity Partners in August of this year. Some analysts believe the decision to close the BioWare was "entirely predictable." For now, BioWare and the Mass Effect game franchise seem to be without a future . In the wake of decision making by EA leadership, fans quickly launched a petition to save the series and amassed more than 50,000 signatures . A trailer for the now-canceled Mass Effect 5 also quickly leaked online .

Michael Cripe is a freelance writer with IGN. He's best known for his work at sites like The Pitch, The Escapist, and OnlySP. Be sure to give him a follow on Bluesky (@mikecripe.bsky.social) and Twitter (@MikeCripe).

articles.title: Nintendo Legend Shigeru Miyamoto Becomes First Game Designer to Be Awarded Japan's Order of Culture
articles.summary: Innovative and prolific Nintendo game developer Shigeru Miyamoto will receive Japan’s highest honor for cultural merit next month. The 73-year old is the first video game developer to receive the Order of Culture, which is presented by the Emperor of Japan.
articles.body:
Legendary Nintendo designer Shigeru Miyamoto will receive Japan’s highest honor for cultural merit next month. The 73-year old is the first video game developer to receive the Order of Culture, which is presented by the Emperor of Japan.

“I feel incredibly awkward but truly honored to be selected for such a prestigious award,” Miyamoto told the press on October 23. “As I often point out, I don’t create games on my own. This award is the result of working together with a great number of people, so I will accept it on their behalf.”

“Recently, I’ve been privileged to work with people from many different fields, not just games,” he added, referencing Super Nintendo World attractions at Universal Studios and films like The Super Mario Galaxy Movie. “I’d like to share the joy of this award with everyone.”

Miyamoto is currently Nintendo’s Executive Fellow and Representative Director. He joined the company in 1977, playing a pivotal and formative role in Nintendo’s move towards making video games. While most famous for creating the Mario series (with the iconic Nintendo mascot’s first appearance in 1981’s Donkey Kong), Miyamoto also played key roles in the development of other major Nintendo franchises including The Legend of Zelda and Star Fox.

“50 years ago, I became involved in video games, a medium whose form was still very undefined, and I have been fortunate to continue in this line of work ever since.” Miyamoto said. “I feel like it’s precisely because I’ve been here since the dawn of the industry that I’m being honored in this way, and think I have been incredibly lucky in life.”

Japan’s Order of Culture, as the name suggests, is awarded to individuals deemed to have made outstanding contributions to the development of culture. It covers a broad scope, from the sciences to literature and the arts. Previous well-known recipients include film director Akira Kurosawa, fashion designer Issey Miyake, and Godzilla composer Akira Ifukube.

The Emperor of Japan will present Miyamoto and the other seven recipients with their Order of Culture awards. Like in previous years, the ceremony will be held on November 3, Japan’s Culture Day national holiday.

Photo by Kevin Winter/GA/The Hollywood Reporter via Getty Images.

Verity Townsend is a Japan-based freelance writer who previously served as editor, contributor and translator for the game news site Automaton West. She has also written about Japanese culture and movies for various publications.

articles.title: Humble Bundle’s Sci-Fi Exposure Bundle Is Stacked With 8 Games for $25, Including Marathon
articles.summary: To celebrate its 15th anniversary, Humble Bundle has dropped a new Sci-Fi Exposure Bundle which features 8 thrilling sci-fi games – including Bungie's Marathon – which you can get for as low as $25.
articles.body:
Humble Bundle is celebrating its 15th anniversary with a new Sci-Fi Exposure bundle that features Bungie's Marathon , RoboCop: Rogue City , Ghostrunner , and 5 more games. For as low as $25, you can add all 8 of them (which you can see below) to your Steam library, which sure beats paying the usual total cost for all of them together at $375, if you ask me. It's only available for another 20 days, though, so the countdown has begun to add this stack of sci-fi games to your PC library.

Humble Bundle 15th Anniversary Sci-Fi Exposure Bundle

Humble 15th Anniversary - Sci-Fi Exposure Bundle

If you want to pay more than $25 for this bundle, you can actually send a little extra cash to Humble, publishers, and a charity called charity: water, which is a non-profit that helps bring clean drinking water to people in developing countries. From Humble's main page for this bundle, you can also adjust your donation to choose how much money you want to send and to where, which is helpful so you can know where it's going.

On the other hand, paying less than $25 nets you fewer games from the bundle. So, if you decide to pay at least $15, you'll get six games from the lineup instead, which are Crysis 3 Remastered, Crysis 2 Remastered, Crysis Remastered, RoboCop: Rogue City - Collection, Ghostrunner 2, and Ghostrunner. If you drop below that to $10, you'll only get RoboCop: Rogue City - Collection, Ghostrunner 2, and Ghostrunner, so you're missing out on quite a few exciting games, including Marathon.

This game is certainly one of the standouts of this bundle. It's one we had a great time playing, with writer Travis Northup calling it "a ruthless and unforgiving extraction shooter that’s worth every ounce of hell it puts you through" in his 9/10 review.

Both Ghostrunner and Ghostrunner 2 earned high praise from us as well - scores of 8 and 9, respectively - and even RoboCop: Rogue City is a game we consider "the video game equivalent of a B movie in the best way," landing with a score of 7/10. So, no matter which game you jump into from this bundle's lineup, you're sure to have an excellent time booting it up on PC.

Humble has had quite a few great bundles popping up lately that are worth checking out alongside this one. Looking for a little something to play for Halloween? The Cozy After Dark Showcase Bundle is full of some delightfully spooky picks. There's also the Double Fine Publisher Bundle , which features some excellent titles like Psychonauts and Brutal Legend to play. And of course, the October Humble Choice is well worth a look while it's still live.

Hannah Hoolihan is a freelancer who writes with the commerce team here at IGN.

articles.body:
DC Studios' horror flick Clayface - which we called a "fun, gritty and gruesome throwback" in our review - is out in cinemas today, but that's not all. Select retailers have also officially dropped preorders for its Blu-ray , 4K , and 4K Steelbook , which is great news if you're excited to grab a physical copy.

As is the case with most early preorders like this one, there's no set release date for it and no news on bonus features just yet. Once they're announced, though, we'll be sure to add them here. Clayface (Limited Edition 4K Ultra HD Steelbook + Blu-ray + Digital)

The cover for Clayface's steelbook is quite cool. On the front, which is bright red, you've got half of Matt's face which is melting off, and if you flip it over, you'll find the other half of his face looking fine and normal. You can get a closer look at both sides in the image below, alongside the steelbook's inside cover.

If you're eager to catch this one in theaters, though (and the timing couldn't be better during spooky season, really), you're sure to have a great time. articles.title: BioWare May Be Gone, But Its Spirit Lives On in These Games
articles.summary: BioWare was shut down by EA earlier this week. While the studio had struggled through a long stretch without putting out a genuine classic, it’s no lie to say it was behind some of the best RPGs of all time. At its peak, with games like Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, Mass Effect and Dragon Age: Origins, BioWare was a pioneer of not only building worlds, but filling those worlds with characters I (and so many others) actually cared about.
articles.body:
BioWare was shut down by EA earlier this week . While the studio had struggled through a long stretch without putting out a genuine classic, it’s no lie to say it was behind some of the best RPGs of all time . At its peak, with games like Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic , Mass Effect and Dragon Age: Origins , BioWare was a pioneer of not only building worlds, but filling those worlds with characters I (and so many others) actually cared about.

But BioWare went so much further than just writing some witty dialog and calling it a day. I always think back to the Mass Effect 2’s climactic suicide mission, where, unless you’ve completed all of your companions’ loyalty quests and built up those relationships, there was a real chance they would just die, never to return in the trilogy’s final chapter. BioWare built personal, heartbreaking consequences into its stories.

The games BioWare made in its heyday were incredibly influential, but I don’t think there are any games from other developers that tried to build on those successes that truly hit the same level. Even BioWare struggled to capture that same magic in its latter games. But while I don’t think there is anything out there close to the ultimate quality of the Mass Effect trilogy or the first three Dragon Age games, the spirit of BioWare’s best work does live on in the work of the games they inspired.

Just in the last few years, there have been plenty of games that draw straight from BioWare’s well, and there are quite a few projects in the works, including two that look like they could just be new BioWare games. So if you’re hunting for more BioWare in the wake of this terrible news, here are six games to keep in mind.

All Origin Characters in Baldur's Gate 3

Now, obviously BioWare made the first two Baldur’s Gate games, so of course they had a massive influence on the third one. But each time I go back to Larian’s Baldur’s Gate 3 , the influence from Mass Effect and Dragon Age becomes more obvious. The way it introduces your companions and encourages you to build close relationships, for example, is extremely BioWare.

That’s not to mention the complicated web of different romance options in the game. I ended up wooing Lae’Zel, and spent hours building her into a reliable tank to carry me through the late game. And then I made a really bad decision involving a mind flayer, and she just straight up left my party for good. I had to figure out how to adjust my party (and my broken heart) from there.

Earlier in that playthrough, I ended up accidentally killing a potential companion, just because of some choices I made when trying to help some fellow paladins in Act One. It wasn’t until my next playthrough that I even realized they were someone I could recruit, and when I did realize it, I felt awful. In many ways, this chain of action and consequence mirrors what I love so much about Mass Effect 2’s suicide mission, but in Baldur’s Gate 3, it spans the entire game.

Even outside your little web of companions, the choices you make are core to what makes Baldur’s Gate 3 tick. From the outset, the game throws seriously consequential decisions your way that can come back to bite you in the ass depending on what you choose to do with them. Early on, there’s a commune of druids that are having a spat with some visiting Tieflings, and the way you handle that doesn’t just affect the scenario, but begins a domino effect that extends through the whole campaign. There are some pretty dark ways that situation can play out, too, and that’s just one of the dozens of encounters you have to deal with that shapes your character and playthrough.

The Outer Worlds: Spacer's Choice Edition Screenshots

Most of the time, The Outer Worlds feels like Fallout: New Vegas in space. That’s a pretty natural conclusion, considering it’s developed by New Vegas studio Obsidian Entertainment. But just like Baldur’s Gate 3, The Outer Worlds frequently feels exactly like a BioWare game, thanks to the way it handles its six companions. No matter how many wild situations the game puts you through, the thing that always sticks with me when I go back to The Outer Worlds is how fleshed out the companions are.

All of them have their own distinct needs, leading to side quest chains that will ultimately decide their fate. And, similar to both Mass Effect and Dragon Age’s decision-tallying finales, there’s an entire tree of different endings that change depending on the choices you make. A lot of the questlines that dictate those endings cross over each other too, creating this tangled web of possibilities that can potentially make every playthrough just a little bit different.

The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered Screenshots

CD Projekt Red and BioWare go way back, with the original Witcher game being built on the same engine as Neverwinter Nights . So, it’s not surprising that The Witcher games have carried the spirit of BioWare’s approach to storytelling for years. And that feels a little weird to say, because when I think of BioWare, I think of RPGs with a protagonist that you create yourself, and companions that surround you for the entire course of the game – two things The Witcher doesn’t have. In all of the Witcher games you play as Geralt of Rivia and, occasionally, other characters from the books, and the allies you gather aren’t party companions in the BioWare sense of the word.

I go back and forth with myself all the time over which of these games I love the most, but The Witcher 3 is probably the best example of CDPR taking BioWare’s legacy and running with it. You spend most of your time in The Witcher 3 on your own, trying to find Geralt’s adoptive daughter, Ciri. But even though you are by yourself most of the time, there’s a huge focus on doing side missions for supporting characters to build up allegiances ahead of when – spoilers – the villainous Wild Hunt attacks your fortress home of Kaer Morhen. Right off the bat, that leaves a lot of potential for an ending reminiscent of Mass Effect 2’s iconic final mission, but unfortunately not a lot happens if you fail to recruit friends to help defend the Witcher fortress.

Still, The Witcher 3 is a game I’ve played through four or five times, and even though I know there’s not much of a gameplay purpose to recruiting everyone, I still try to get all my friends into that castle in the mountains, even if it just means unlocking dialog that makes me feel warm and fuzzy.

It’s no secret that for the last decade or so, even before EA shuttered BioWare, things were rough for the studio. A lot of talented people jumped ship, especially in the run-up to Anthem. One of the studios that formed from these talented ex-BioWare folks is Archetype Entertainment, and its first game, Exodus , is due out on April 7 next year.

We’ve actually got the chance to play a bit of Exodus early, and from what I’ve seen and read from my colleagues, it looks as much like a new Mass Effect game as yesterday’s leaked trailer. It’s a squad-based sci-fi RPG, and one of your squadmates is an octopus in a giant mech. That sounds ridiculous, and it is, but just look at the wild and wonderful companions we got in Mass Effect. In the trailer we got at Gamescom, there were scenes that made it look like we’re going to meet their family. So, it at least seems like there’s going to be some suitably wild companion quests in the game.

Crucially, though, Exodus has Drew Karpyshyn as its Narrative Director, and that is more exciting for me than any amount of marketing. This is the guy who wrote the original Mass Effect and Knights of the Old Republic, two of BioWare’s all-time best games. Karpyshyn leaving BioWare was, as far as I’m concerned, the biggest red flag that Anthem wasn’t going to turn out well, and while I’m not happy that my gut feeling was right there, at least we can see what he’s been working on for the last five years in just a few months.

The Expanse: Osiris Reborn: Exclusive Progression Screenshots

Just like Exodus, The Expanse: Osiris Reborn is another spiritual successor to Mass Effect, although its scope is maybe a little less fantastic. It’s based on, well, The Expanse, the popular hard sci-fi novels and their TV show adaptation, so it already has a deep well of lore to draw from, and there’s a ton of potential there. Probably. I’m going to be honest, I haven’t read any of the books or watched the show, so I don’t really know much about the world of Osiris Reborn.

But I am familiar with Owlcat Games, which has been making some of the biggest cult-favorite RPGs of the last few years. Most recently, it made Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader, an excellent, deep CRPG set in Games Workshop’s 40K universe. But while Owlcat knows how to make a rich RPG, Osiris Reborn is the studio’s first foray into making an Action RPG with realtime third-person shooter combat, and its wearing Mass Effect’s influence on its sleeve for all to see.

It does look like Osiris Reborn is going to be a bit more narrow in scope compared to Exodus, with less aliens and time dilation shenanigans, and more of a focus on politics and your own personal struggle. But from everything I’ve seen of the game, it still feels like a Mass Effect game, from the way you choose dialog options to the squad-based combat.

I’m not sure when The Expanse: Osiris Reborn is actually going to arrive. Right now, it just has a vague ‘Q2 2027’ release date on Steam, so hopefully I’m able to get my hands on it before summer. But, even if it does get delayed, maybe it’ll give me a chance to actually watch the show and read some of the novels to brush up on the lore.

Star Wars Fate of the Old Republic Screenshots

Star Wars: Fate of the Old Republic was revealed nearly a year ago at The Game Awards 2025, and at this point we still don’t know much about it. The teaser looks awesome, and shows a jedi on some desolate planet looking angry as she walks into some mysterious room. Not a lot to go on there. So it would usually be a bit too early to really say that this game will carry on the spirit of BioWare, but it just so happens that it’s helmed by Casey Hudson, who directed the original Mass Effect trilogy and Knights of the Old Republic.

In the press release shared by the newly-founded Arcanaut Studios when it announced the game, it says its “crafting an adventure about choice, destiny, and the timeless struggle between light and dark.” And even without seeing any of the gameplay or how conversations with NPCs will look, it sounds like it’s a true successor to Knights of the Old Republic. It’s important to remember that in a lot of ways, Mass Effect was also a spiritual successor to KOTOR, and I expect a lot of the DNA from that game is going to carry over into this new Star Wars RPG.

The catch, though, is that while Osiris Reborn has some shaky ‘Q2 2027’ release date looming over it, I have no idea when Fate of the Old Republic is going to see the light of day. Hudson did come out and respond to people that were memeing about the game not coming out until 2030 , where he said it’d be coming out a bit sooner than that. But with a game of this scope, I’d be surprised if we saw it before 2028.

Regardless, the prospect of a big Star Wars RPG directed by Casey Hudson with everything he learned from Mass Effect is exciting. It’s still early, but even though I’ve seen very little, this is probably the one I’m most excited about, it just sucks that it’s the one we have to wait the longest for.

articles.title: Inde Navarrette Reveals Sneak Peek at Her Rogue Accent Ahead of X-Men Debut
articles.summary: Inde Navarrette revealed a sneak peek at her Rogue accent in a new video featuring her take on the X-Men hero's iconic "sugar" catchphrase, but she's willing to "work on it" if fans don't like it.
articles.body:
Inde Navarrette revealed a sneak peek at her Rogue accent in a new video featuring her take on the X-Men hero's iconic "sugah" catchphrase, but she's willing to "work on it" if fans don't like it.

One of the many stars confirmed to appear in the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU) X-Men reboot movie gave fans a taste of the big reveal that everyone's been waiting on: her take on Rogue's accent. Navarrette offered just a single "sugah" when asked for a tease during an interview with Etalk at TIFF 2026 last month.

The Obsession breakout admitted she's not "done a lot of practice" when it comes to her Rogue preparation, but it looks like she has spent at least some time fitting a more recognizable word from her vocabulary into her performance. You can see the clip of Navarrette in question below.

Rogue is known for her sense of style and power-sapping abilities, but it might be her accent that fans know her for best. With Navarrette confirmed to play the Mississippi-born mutant when X-Men joins the MCU in 2028, fans have been dying to hear what she'll sound like – and she knows it.

In September, she assured Rogue fans that she was putting in the work to, above all else, nail that Southern delivery . Part of her plan to do so involved planning a trip to Mississippi at some point in the future, saying at the time that "Southern women are really my favorite." She also went on to say that she was "doing everything humanly possible" to do Rogue justice because she "loves that character."

Rogue has appeared in animated and live-action form before, but her introduction into the MCU could be her most important portrayal yet. Navarrette is all too aware of what she and her roots mean to fans, so if you don't like that quick "sugah" she teased last month, she promised she'll iron out the kinks with Marvel Studios.

"I that, you know, I'm going to work on it if you don't like it," she said, "and I'm going to figure out and talk to the Marvel team on what we want to do."

Following months of Mystique rumors, Navarrette was confirmed to play Rogue when Marvel appeared for a special announcement at D23 in August . She was joined by a host of other cast confirmations, including Christopher Abbott as Professor X and Maya Boyd as Storm, too. Asa Germann was cast as Angel not much longer after.

X-Men will reimagine classic Marvel superheroes for the big screen when it comes to theaters May 5, 2028. Until then, you can see how Rogue's animated voice actor, Lenore Zann, reacted to Navarrette's casting . You can also read up on the comic book stories director Jake Schreier is keeping in mind while working on the project .

articles.title: Yaga’s First Two Episodes Pull You in Deeply, Begging You to Experience the Rest of the Series as Its Secrets and Mysteries Are Uncovered
articles.summary: Yaga Premiere Review: Kat Sandler’s retelling of the Slavic witchy folktale will have you grasping for more clues in the dark, while your jaw is dropped wide open.
articles.body:
Warning: This review contains full spoilers for Yaga Season 1, Episodes 1-2. Both episodes are now streaming on AMC+ in the US and Crave in Canada.

For anyone familiar with the Eastern European folktale of Baba Yaga, you might have visions of a wicked old witch in the woods who lives in a hut made out of chicken feet. In reality, Baba Yaga is a complex character who can harness the role of both villain and mentor, depending on the story, and encompasses both good and evil.

Yaga, the new series from Kat Sandler, who wrote a stage play with the same title, is a modern retelling of the folktale of Baba Yaga itself. The first two episodes offer an alternate version of the traditional lore, as Yaga dives head first into seduction and horror, while sprinkling humor throughout amid many twists that make you question what’s real, what’s something else entirely, and what that “something else” even is. (Sounds weird, right? Good.)

The opening of Episode 1 sets the tone for where the show seems to be heading. It begins with narration from Baba Yaga herself, describing in detail how she has been perceived in tales “as wicked as the night and as wise and powerful as the sea” – a creature who eats children’s guts and bones and is too ugly to be desired by anyone. But there’s an underlying warning to her ramble.

Nighttime shots are mixed throughout the monologue, ending with Baba Yaga saying, “But the thing that really gets me… is this.” Cut to a man in a forest standing in the middle of a large bonfire, screaming while he’s being burned alive.

We then go straight into meeting the main characters of Whittock, a small Pacific Northwest-esque island town, and dive into the basics of the story: Charlie Rapp, played by Noah Reid (Schitt’s Creek, The Vampire Lestat), and Sergeant Carson, played by Clark Backo (Letterkenny, The Changeling), are forced to team up to investigate the disappearance of Henry Park, played by Hudson Williams (Heated Rivalry) – a billionaire playboy whose family is well-known in the town. Rapp was hired on by the Park family to find their son and seems to have questionable intentions for working on the case, which Carson is immediately suspicious of.

We next meet Logan Casey, Henry’s roommate – also played by Williams – who surprisingly looks just like Henry, albeit with a seemingly different demeanor and minor physical changes. Logan acts like he’s hiding something as Carson and Rapp look through the house, though he lets it slip that Rapp and Henry know each other, and Rapp doesn’t seem to appreciate the revelation.

The investigation continues in town, with Carson wondering if Henry’s actually even missing. Carson also accuses Rapp of flirting with basically every single woman he sees, and at first glance, it is possible to dismiss Rapp as a dumb flirt, but as you get further into these first two episodes, his eye-batting tendencies are revealed as a tactic to dig up more dirt (well, most of the time).

Eventually, Rapp meets a woman, Katherine Hargrove (The Matrix’s Carrie-Anne Moss) in an upscale bar. He immediately hits on her and she pulls him right into her orbit – feeling him out with sexy, teasing comments. As Katherine, Moss evokes an intoxicating, seductive quality where you just want to know more about her – and what she’s hiding.

Throughout the first episode, Rapp continuously texts Henry asking where he is and if he’s alright. In a sudden twist, the episode wraps with Rapp finally getting texts back from Henry saying, “STOP LOOKING FOR ME.”

Over the course of these premiere episodes, we see clues from the investigation come into play, specifically images from Henry’s bedroom pointing to people who Rapp and Carson have associated with, including an obscure witch-like symbol, expensive vintage watches, photos, and chicken feet.

Speaking of which, there’s also a consistent, somewhat odd, yet seemingly calculated theme throughout the episodes: chickens. From a chicken foot being tied to Henry’s bedpost, to Carson hitting a chicken with his car while driving through the woods and Rapp snapping its neck to put it out of its misery (which, in turn, haunts him with hallucinations), to even finding a chicken lit on fire and nailed to the door of Rapp’s motel room while he’s getting intimate with a woman named Angel, chickens are everywhere.

By Episode 2, Rapp admits to Carson that he’s definitely friends with Henry – we don’t know how close of friends though – while various people in town who the cop duo are questioning seem increasingly suspicious about the “disappearance” of Henry. Are all these town characters somehow in on Henry’s vanishing? Is there something else going on, something altogether darker?

One of those people is Katherine, who we find out is a professor at the university Henry attends, and who numerous people refer to as the “Boner Beast” due to her allegedly having sex with students. However, she rejects the nickname, stating she’s known as more specifically the “Bone Beast” due to her studies in osteology.

We get the biggest twist so far in the last part of Episode 2, where we see Rapp and Carson going undercover at a “dark solstice party” Henry is apparently hosting at his house – despite his “disappearance” – complete with masks, dark mood lighting, and electronic music. Soon we see what looks to be Henry standing at the upper level railing wearing devil horns while looking down over his partygoers.

As Rapp and Carson search throughout the party for him, we see another shot of someone who seems to be Henry upstairs in his room, having sex with a woman against his photo wall while wearing a leather dog mask – she’s wearing ethereal angel wings and the scene gives a sultry nod to the duality of light and darkness… an angel and a devil.

At this same time, Rapp runs into Angel, who offers a lollipop dipped into a powder, possibly ecstasy, which he willingly accepts. Carson grabs Rapp while reprimanding his insane choices, and they head upstairs to continue their search for Henry. Soon, Rapp hears faint moaning coming from one of the rooms. The person who we now believe to be Henry demands the woman he’s with to say his name while they are continuing to have sex, and she shouts out “Henry!” multiple times, causing Rapp and Carson to instantly look at each other, confirming their suspicions.

Rapp kicks open the door and Henry sees him and panics, running out of the room and shoving Carson in the process as he escapes into the hallway.

As Henry is in the hallway, someone who resembles him seems to magically split apart from his body and run down the stairs while the other one takes off the mask and goes into the bathroom. However, we’re seeing this through Rapp’s point of view, and the drugs he took earlier might be affecting his vision, so he doesn’t notice one of the people going into the bathroom and follows who he believes to be Henry running down the stairs.

Carson is still upstairs at this point and sees Logan come out of the bathroom, despite thinking it was Henry who ran in there. As she tries to grab him to talk with him, he pushes her face into the wall and yells, “Fucking stay out of this!” and runs into his room nearby. Carson follows, but finds him nowhere in the small room. It’s like he magically disappeared out of thin air.

Rapp makes his way outside at a slow-moving pace (due to him hallucinating from the drugs he took) when he sees a vision of Katherine in a white dress with a white mask over her face as she speaks softly to him. He comes back to reality when Carson calls his name, snapping open his eyes and then seeing a large bird flying across the sky, lit on fire – but we don’t know for sure if what he is seeing is real or imagined.

In the final shot of Episode 2, we hear a shriek followed by a lifeless, naked body lying face down on the nearby shore. We pull back to reveal that the person the body belongs to is Logan. It’s a grim ending with dozens of questions left unanswered. What do you mean Logan is dead? And was he ever really alive? And where did Henry escape to – or was he never really there?

It’s often hard to find a show that makes you linger on so many questions: Is Katherine Baba Yaga or is that too obvious? Are Henry and Logan actually the same person but magically split in two? Is Baba Yaga creating visions for Rapp? Was Henry the one burning in the fire at the beginning of Episode 1? We don't have answers yet, but I’m ready and waiting for more reveals from this supernatural story that has already sunk its iron teeth into me.

Jessie Wade is Associate Director of Editorial Programming at IGN. You can find her watching the latest rom-com and drama shows, as well as getting lost in too many books. Ones that involve fantastical creatures and queer storytelling are preferred. For games, you can find her playing the latest cozy indies and fantasy RPG's.

articles.title: Acer's New $1299 Predator Atlas 8 Intel Arc G3 Extreme Handheld Gaming PC Is Now Available at Best Buy
articles.summary: Aims to topple the Ryzen Z2 Extreme from its throne.
articles.body:
The wait is over. A handheld gaming PC equipped with Intel's new Intel Arc G3 Extreme graphics is now available at a price that's going to give Z2 Extreme handhelds a run for their money. Starting October 23, Best Buy is accepting orders of the new Acer Predator Atlas 8 handheld gaming PC . As of this post, orders are shipping out immediately. Best of all, the launch price is pegged at $1,299.99. That makes it a hugely competitive alternative to the ASUS ROG Xbox Ally X20 , which costs the same price, and the Legion Go 2 , which costs $700 more.

New Release: Acer Predator Atlas 8 Handheld Gaming PC

Acer Predator Atlas 8 Intel Arc G3 Extreme Handheld Gaming PC

Let's get this out the way first: the Intel Arc G3 Extreme is powerful . It's built on the Intel Core Ultra Series 3 Panther Lake platform and features 14 cores, 14 threads, and a max turbo frequency of 4.7GHz. In real world usage, it's significantly more powerful than the AMD Ryzen Z2 Extreme . We haven't yet reviewed the Acer variant, but Jacqueline Thomas did review the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ handheld , which is also equipped with the Arc G3 Extreme. That handheld "blew every Z2 Extreme-powered device out of the water," with performance improvements by as much as 40%. It was powerful enough to run most games at up to 60fps on the 1200p display. The only problem? The MSI Claw 8 EX cost $1800. Fortunately, the Acer Predator Atlas 8 is much, much less expensive.

As for the rest of the specs, the Acer Predator Atlas 8 features a spacious 8" IPS screen with 1920x1200 resolution, up to 120Hz refresh rate with VRR, 500nits of peak brightness, and Corning Gorilla Glass Victus with DXC protection. The CPU is supported by 24GB of LPDDR5X RAM and a 512GB internal SSD with MicroSD card expansion. The controls have been updated with TMR non-contact drift-resistant joysticks and dual-mode Hall Effect triggers.

Connectivity options include two USB 3.2 Gen 2x2 Type-C ports supporting DisplayPort 2.1 and Thunderbolt 4 with 65W of Power Delivery, MicroSD expansion slot, and a headphone jack. On the wireless front you get Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4.

At this price I don't know how long the Acer Predator Atlas 8 will stay in stock. Since it's priced very aggressively at a time when most gaming PCs trend the other direction, and with the holiday shopping season fast approaching, I wouldn't be surprised if this handheld gets hard to find quickly.
